text: Cassini had used almost all of its fuel by the end of the mission, so it could not steer itself onto a controlled landing. The concern was that if it accidentally hit Enceladus or Titan, Earth microorganisms might survive there. Diving into Saturn was the safest end state. Saturn’s atmosphere and gravity would strip and shred the craft, scattering it through the upper atmosphere and the rings. The planet is large enough that contamination of a moon becomes negligible. So the crash was planned, and it kept the candidate habitats clean because Saturn is not considered habitable, it was acceptable.

If your stationary leg aches, it usually means that side is being loaded more than you expect. On a skateboard, the leg on the board may look still, but it's supporting your weight, taking the bumps, and holding your balance. The pushing leg, even when planted, is doing the work of moving you, so quads, glutes, hip flexors, ankles and knees are repeatedly loaded. That is a common source of muscle soreness or joint irritation, especially when you're new or have increased distance.

A lot of pain comes from technique. People bend the knee too much, push with a locked knee, or swing the leg with the hip instead of extending through the whole chain. That can irritate muscles, tendons, or joints. It could be ordinary eccentric soreness, but sharp knee, hip, or ankle pain, swelling, or difficulty bending or straightening the joint means think more seriously. The board leg can also get fatigued from impact and repeated pressure on the foot and ankle. Weak or cold muscles are more likely to hurt, so warm up, keep the hip and knee in line, and strengthen glutes, quads, hamstrings, and calves. If the ache fades with rest and better form, it's probably overuse. If it lingers more than a couple of days, get it checked. Check your shoes; thin or damaged soles transmit more shock to the ankle and knee. If you push in the cold or at night, start gently and allow more rest days between sessions. Another factor is the difference between the two legs over time: if you always use the same leg to push, that side accumulates more strain, while the board leg also absorbs board impacts. Rotating legs and keeping push distance shorter reduces the load on any one side. This protects your joints over time.

The term is not saying that most Black Americans are currently from Africa, or that they have no other ancestry. It is a broad identity label for people with significant African descent in the United States. That descent often comes from the millions of Africans brought here during the transatlantic slave trade, so many Black Americans have ancestors from West and Central Africa even if they themselves were born and raised in the U.S. The label also includes people of Caribbean, Latin American, and mixed African heritage. It is less about where someone lives now and more about shared history and cultural experience. Some Black Americans have little or no direct connection to a particular African country, and that does not make the term wrong; it just means the term is a general one, not a precise ethnic or geographic description. It is also used in politics and everyday speech to mark a common social category, especially in the U.S. context. People can use it as a way to claim belonging without needing a specific African national origin. That is the practical point: it is an identity umbrella, not an exact census field.

Mostly they come from nearby states, regional dealers, and small local workshops rather than one single official channel. In recent years, some factions have imported through cross-border traders, while others have built or repaired arms locally. They keep getting them because armed groups still need weapons to hold territory, recruit fighters, and signal strength. The state’s weakened monopoly on force means militias and regional backers can maintain arsenals. Factions also use weapons to attract supporters and to keep rivals off-balance. So long as the political settlement remains incomplete, weapons keep flowing as a tool of negotiation and self-protection.

There is no hard rule that says every drug must be bad; the rule is closer to “stronger central effects usually mean stronger adaptation and risk.” Euphoric drugs act on brain reward, calming, or arousal systems. Those systems are not isolated. A molecule that binds strongly and changes neurotransmitter signaling will push the brain to compensate. With cocaine, dopamine signal increases, and repeated use tends to shrink the brain’s response and create craving. With opioids, the body changes receptor sensitivity, so stopping leads to withdrawal. Alcohol works on GABA and glutamate, and its effects are a sliding scale from relaxation to sedation and toxicity.

The phrase “bad” does one job: it lumps together many different harms. Some come from the drug molecule, some from how much and how often, and some from the person using it. A person who can handle one substance does not handle everything else. Liver enzymes, kidney function, age, sleep, and mental health all change how a drug behaves. That is why there is no universal “good” or “bad” drug; there is a risk profile.

A zero-adverse-effect pleasure drug would need to produce a big signal in a narrow system without spilling into others. In practice, intense feelings depend on widespread receptor changes. The brain treats big, repeated signals as something to balance out, which creates tolerance. If you want the same high later, you take more, and the margin for error shrinks. The same mechanism can also produce dependence or withdrawal.

There are substances that seem milder, but “milder” is not “harmless.” Cannabis, alcohol, and some stimulants can be used with lower risk for some people, yet they can still affect mood, sleep, memory, and motivation. The claim that every drug is bad is a simplification, but the claim that an intense euphoric drug could be perfectly harmless is the harder claim. The brain’s reward circuits are shared with pain, motivation, and alertness. A powerful euphoria is a strong perturbation, and strong perturbations generally carry costs.

Maybe there are safer molecules, and science keeps improving them. But if a drug really produced intense pleasure with zero adverse effects, we would not be debating it here. It would be in trials.

Hi,

I get it. The pain you're feeling is probably because your body has to stay on its feet and move around for hours, carry bags, and endure the constant stop-start crowds. That is different from an ordinary headache because it is cumulative physical strain. If the pain is in your head, it's likely a tension headache from stress, poor posture, or not drinking enough. Your legs, back and neck tense up while you're busy. It is real, not in your head. You're not alone.

Try taking short breaks, wearing proper footwear, and drinking water.

Cheers

That’s all there is to it.

Hi Maya,

I’m glad you asked before signing anything. The first thing to settle is how much you can actually afford, not just what the bank will lend. Add mortgage, property tax, insurance, maintenance, and closing costs. A good rule is to keep total housing costs under 30% of take-home pay, and leave a buffer.

Before you get attached to a property, get an independent inspection and check for hidden problems, flood risk, and the condition of the roof and foundations. Also review the title and deed carefully; surprises there are expensive. A local solicitor should review the sale contract, and you should understand every clause before paying a deposit. Ask for the service charge and ground rent details too, plus council tax.

If you share your specific questions, I’ll answer each one in turn. In the meantime, start by making a list of must-have features, then compare at least a dozen homes before falling in love with one. Get pre-approved so you know your ceiling, and negotiate anything that comes up in the inspection. Bring your bank pre-approval letter before viewing too.

Let’s have a quick call this weekend if you want to go through it together.

Talk soon,
Sam

The difference is mainly in formulation, not just branding. A 3-in-1 must work on both skin and hair, so it combines cleansing surfactants with conditioning agents such as cationic polymers, emollients, or silicones. Those actives are supposed to deposit on hair and give slip and softness without heavy buildup. The problem is that a single formula has to compromise: its surfactants are usually milder than a dedicated shampoo so they can be used on skin, and its conditioning load is lighter than a dedicated conditioner. Compared with a 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner, adding a bodywash role pushes the formula toward a broader, all-purpose use. In practice, a 3-in-1 is less aggressive as a cleanser and less intensive as a conditioner than separate products. It is convenient for travel, but it is not the same as using a strong dedicated cleanser plus a proper conditioner. Formulators also have to watch pH. Shampoos are often mildly acidic to help hair cuticles lay flat, while body cleansers tend to be milder or more neutral for skin. A 3-in-1 has to find a middle ground, which is why it can feel less slick or less restorative than a separate conditioner.

Best,
Your name

Hi there,

Nice question. The short answer is that we measure the motion of the crust with geodetic observations, and the main tool is GPS.

Scientists install or use existing GPS reference stations at fixed points on land. Each station records its Earth centered coordinates many times. When those coordinates are compared weeks, months, or years apart, the difference divided by the elapsed time gives a velocity. That velocity is usually in millimeters per year, because continents move slowly.

This does not just measure the whole continent as one rigid object. The crust deforms, so different stations can move at different speeds and directions. A network of stations lets researchers build models of plate motion and regional deformation. They can also combine GPS with InSAR satellite radar data and other geodetic techniques to monitor deformation over larger areas.

For continental plates, the speed is not a single number; it depends on where you look and what reference frame you choose.

The reference frame matters. GPS coordinates are usually described in a terrestrial reference frame, so the measured motion is relative to that frame.

Hope that makes it clear. Let me know if you want the technical details.

Cheers,
Alex

Inbreeding lowers average IQ mainly because it raises the chance that harmful recessive genes become active. Any two gene copies are sometimes identical because the parents share a common ancestor. When close relatives reproduce, more gene copies are likely to be identical, so recessive mutations hidden while paired with a normal copy can be expressed. IQ is influenced by many genes, each with small effects. The added homozygosity increases the chance of combining slightly harmful variants, which can reduce neural development and cognitive ability. Mating between relatives also reduces the variety of alleles available to the child, making harmful combinations more probable.

This is a population-level effect. It does not mean every child will score below average. It means the group average tends to fall because the extra risk of inheriting and expressing bad alleles is higher. Reduced genetic diversity also causes inbreeding depression, which lowers overall fitness and performance.

The body is not evenly wired for pain. Some skin, muscle, and soft tissue contain fewer pain-sensitive nerve endings than other places. The arm is less densely packed with them than the trunk, the face, or areas close to vital organs and major joints. That is why a hit or cut to the arm can feel more tolerable. Pain perception also depends on what was injured and how badly. A stab through the arm may hurt less than a similar injury to the chest or abdomen because those areas have more receptors and protect essential structures. The arm is also mobile, so the person can move it to relieve pressure. This does not mean an arm injury is harmless. It can still need care, and damage to muscle, tendon, bone, or nerves can make it painful. The difference is mostly about nerve density and location, not the type of injury.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it fits the same part of hemoglobin as oxygen, and it holds on much more tightly. When you breathe in CO, it takes the place of oxygen in red blood cells. The bound CO keeps the blood from carrying enough oxygen to the heart, brain, and muscles. This is why a small amount of CO can cause headache, dizziness, and confusion before you notice it. It is a silent danger because the air does not smell or feel different.

Carbon dioxide is not a poison at normal levels because your body makes it all the time and your lungs remove it. It is a normal byproduct of breathing. In fact, a little extra CO2 is how the body knows to breathe harder. Only when CO2 builds up in the blood does it become harmful, a condition called hypercapnia. At normal levels, it does not compete with oxygen for hemoglobin the way carbon monoxide does. That is the core reason for the difference: CO steals oxygen-carrying capacity, while CO2 is mostly a useful internal signal that the lungs normally clear out.

Another important difference is detection. CO has no smell or color, so you may feel fine until the oxygen level drops. CO2, on the other hand, triggers a strong urge to breathe harder. That urge protects you before levels become dangerous. In severe cases, however, too much CO2 can itself make breathing slow and cause loss of consciousness. So CO2 is not poisonous under ordinary conditions, but it is not harmless if it accumulates. CO is poisonous even at low levels because hemoglobin binds it so tightly, while CO2 is mainly a normal signal that the lungs normally remove. This matters for us because both gases are invisible, so good ventilation and working alarms are protection.

In an aircraft emergency, the brace position is a specific body posture passengers and crew are taught to assume when impact is imminent or suspected. Its purpose is to reduce the chance that the body is thrown forward or twisted in a way that causes serious injury. By tucking the head down, pulling the chin to the chest, keeping arms crossed or holding the seat in front, and bending the knees slightly, the body becomes more compact and stable. This helps the neck, back, and limbs absorb force more evenly and keeps them from hitting the seat in front or the floor with full momentum. The idea is simple: in a sudden deceleration, unrestrained body parts keep moving forward. Bracing turns that momentum into a controlled, shorter movement, so the spine, neck, and joints are less likely to be overstretched, dislocated, or snapped.

The position is not meant to make a crash safe, but it can lower injury risk. If impact happens while the body is already braced, the force is spread across the chest, arms, and legs instead of concentrating on one point. Crew members use the same principle while preparing the cabin, and passengers are coached to keep the position until told otherwise.

Most companies today are relatively young, and the industrial era brought the conditions needed for large modern businesses. Factories, railways, banking and mass markets changed how firms grew. A business that existed long before that era would likely have been very small, local, or family-run, so it would not be well known. Many older firms were also absorbed into larger competitors, or disappeared when markets shifted. It is not that no pre-industrial businesses existed; it is that few survived, and the ones that did stay small and local, so they did not become widely known.

I keep coming back to the idea that a lower rate at the dealer isn't automatically a better deal. The rate is only part of the cost. If the dealer's loan is for six years and the bank's is for three years, the bank can be cheaper in total dollars even with a slightly higher rate. Interest is charged on the balance that is still owed, and a longer term means you are paying interest for more months. That extra time can easily wipe out the rate difference. I've seen the exact same car quoted at two places, and the lower-rate dealer quote had a much longer schedule, so the total interest was higher. The bank's schedule was shorter and had fewer fees, so the all-in cost was lower.

Dealerships also have a habit of burying fees in the deal. A finance charge, a documentation fee, or an optional product can be folded into the principal or added after the headline rate is advertised. The advertised rate looks great, but the fee shows up later. A bank's number is usually more transparent. You get the rate, the term, and the total interest, and you can check it against your budget. I am the sort of person who compares the all-in cost, not the rate, because a few months of extra interest adds up quickly.

My position is that the real question is total cost of credit, not the headline APR. A lower rate at the dealership can be a trap if the term is longer or the fees are hidden. If you want the cheaper financing, compare the total, not the rate. Ask for the payment schedule and the fee breakdown from both places, then do the simple math: total interest plus fees. That is the number that tells you which is actually cheaper. I would always take that number over a pretty interest rate, because the rate by itself does not tell you how long you are paying or what is being hidden in the deal.

California's 2018 recreational law, Colorado's earlier 2012 framework, and New York's 2019 adult-use statute show that marijuana legality is no longer a single national question. It is a patchwork, and I think that patchwork is useful. I support state-by-state legalization because it lets communities choose their own tradeoffs. I have watched small bars in Colorado and California put legal cannabis signs at the door and serve both smokers and nonsmokers, so the choice to go legal gave them a workable path. A federal state is not the right size for one rule. Some states still treat possession as a crime, and others have legalized sale, consumption, and tax collection. The patchwork is messy, but it forces each state to face the question directly. I also like New York's tax, which funds recovery and education, and Washington's 2009 medical rules remain alongside its 2012 recreational law.

My body isn't a battery, but a network of ion pumps. Every cell pushes sodium out and potassium in. This separation makes the outside positive and the inside negative. When a signal reaches a nerve or muscle cell, tiny channels open. Positive sodium rushes in, the inside flips positive for a brief instant, and the current runs along the membrane like a spark. That spark triggers the next section of fiber, which is how a thought can become a movement. The electricity isn't generated at once. It is made continuously by ion movement, and it dies if the pump fails.

I think sampling is less about stealing and more about calling someone into the conversation. When a producer pulls a few seconds of an old record, they are not erasing the original. They are leaving a trace that lets a new track point back to the place where the idea first lived. That is the part I find most interesting. The sample does not replace the original performance. It creates a bridge between eras, and the listener can hear both without either one having to win.

You do not need a huge library to sample. You can find usable material on a scratched CD, a forgotten cassette, or a live broadcast. The key is to treat the source with respect. If the music you like is old enough or obscure enough, you are not fighting a label over every few seconds. You are borrowing a color, a rhythm, or a vocal texture that no one else is using. That makes the new track feel like it belongs to a longer chain of making music.

Technically, the process is simpler than people imagine. You isolate the section you want, clean it up, loop it, and fit it to the tempo of the new song. In a DAW, that can be a few clicks. In an older setup, it could mean bouncing between hardware samplers and tape. The technology changes, but the judgment does not. You still have to listen carefully and know when the sample has stopped helping and started crowding out the new material. A good sample should sit under the new composition, not sit on top of it like an argument.

There is a real ethical center here, and I do not think it is just “pay the rights holder.” It is about recognizing that a sample is a collaboration across time. The original artist created a musical object, and the new artist is treating that object as a starting point. When the sample is prominent, or when the original identity is unmistakable, crediting and compensating the source becomes important. I would rather have a small fee or a shared credit than argue about whether a four-second loop “is” the song. The sample is a conversation, and conversation requires courtesy.

What I find most alive about sampling is the surprise in the combination. Put a dusty 1960s vocal under a heavy drum loop and the old voice suddenly feels urgent and strange. That is not theft. That is a new meaning growing out of an old one. The older song does not disappear. It becomes part of the new music, and the new music carries its memory forward. That is how I see musicians sampling older songs: as a way to keep music in motion by letting the past speak inside the present.

I used to believe my skull was cracking open, but the headache isn't in the bone. The skull itself is bone and doesn't feel much; the pain comes from the stretch and pressure on the soft tissues and blood vessels around the brain. Tension headaches are more like a tight band around the head, while migraines throb in a way that tracks with the pulsing of blood flow.

So when I get one, I stop treating it like my head is physically breaking. I hydrate, take it slow, and give the pressure time to settle. If it keeps happening, seeing someone who can check the vessels and membranes makes more sense than assuming the bone is the culprit.

We can't even say if the food is good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and assumed it would be easy for us. We put our names in their completely useless digital waitlist, were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were even an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. I had assumed the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I figured there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either; it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking at my typing.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well the under-21 version, so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil, not in a rip-off way exactly, just if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The shirts never got there because the sales rep misread her handwritten 7 as a 1. We meant 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people living at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to send it back. It vanished and never turned up again. We did not learn of it for several weeks. While the dispute was going on, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount would not refund the original pair. The owner took over. He admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong house, yet said no refund until the shirts came back. He also put part of the blame on us for not being friendly enough with the 5401 neighbors, just four doors away. We then disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and we eventually received a credit for the first two shirts from the company.
